source: Belfield, S. and Brown, C. (2010). Guidebook on Upland Crops in Cambodia: Corn (សៀវភៅណែនាំ ស្តីពីដំណាំតំបន់ខ្ពង់រាបនៅក្នុងប្រទេសកម្ពុជា៖ ដំណាំពោត). ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
Soil pH strongly affects how available different nutrients are to corn roots (based on the classic pH-availability relationship, University of Kentucky 1970). At low (acidic) pH, aluminium (Al) and manganese (Mn) can become soluble enough to be toxic to roots, while phosphorus, calcium, and molybdenum become less available. At high (alkaline) pH, micronutrients such as zinc, iron, manganese, copper, and boron become less available, potentially causing deficiencies even when total soil levels are adequate.

A soil survey of more than 40 upland sites across Cambodia in 2004-2005, carried out under the ACIAR project, found that most sites were acidic (pH below 5.0 measured in water), commonly low in phosphorus and molybdenum, and often needing additional potassium and magnesium.

Soil pH can be measured either in water (pHw) or in a calcium chloride solution (pHCaCl); the two methods give different numeric values for the same soil, so it's important to know which method a lab result is based on before comparing it to any target range or applying lime recommendations. Where soils are strongly acidic, agricultural lime (calcium carbonate, CaCO3) or dolomitic lime (which also supplies magnesium, CaMg(CO3)2) can be used to raise pH into a range more favourable for nutrient availability and root growth.
